sections.title: Dominant Religions & Beliefs

subsections.title: Roman Catholicism — The Dominant Faith
subsections.content:
- Roman Catholicism is the single largest religious denomination in São Tomé and

Príncipe, constituting an estimated 55.7% of the national population according to the CIA World Factbook's 2012 census -based estimate. Earlier data pointed to higher figures: the  nation's encyclopedia (Britannica) records that over three - quarters of the population was Roman Catholic as of the year 2000, and the Nations Encyclopedia notes a figure of approximately 80% for 2002. The decline in the Catholic share since then reflects the significant growth of Protestant and evangelical denominations, not a general decline in Christian affiliation.

- Catholicism was introduced to the islands by Portuguese colonists from the late

15th century onward. The Diocese of São Tomé and Príncipe —one of Africa's oldest Catholic dioceses —was established by Pope Clement VII on 31 January 1533. At its height, its ju risdiction extended to Catholics in Angola and Mozambique. The first permanent church on the islands, Nossa Senhora da Graça (built in 1504 by Augustinian missionaries), still stands and serves as the Cathedral of São Tomé. Today, the single Catholic dioce se is headquartered in São Tomé city. Index Mundi / CIA World Factbook. Sao Tome and Principe Religions. Available at: https://www.indexmundi.com/sao_tome_and_principe/religions.html  (Accessed: 7 May 2026). Encyclopedia.com. Worldmark Encyclopaedia of Religious Practices: São Tomé and Príncipe. Available at: https://www.encyclopedia.com/religion/encyclopedias - almanacs -transcripts -and-maps/sao -tome -and-principe  (Accessed: 7 May 2026). Wikipedia contributors. subsections.title: Protestant and Evangelical Christianity
subsections.content:
- Protestant Christianity constitutes the second -largest Christian grouping in the

country. The CIA World Factbook (2012) records specific Protestant denominations as follows: Seventh -day Adventist (4.1%), Assembly of God (3.4%), New Apostolic Church (2.9%), Universal Kingdom of God (2%), and Jehovah's Witnesses (1.2%). Evangelical churches have shown significant growth in recent decades owing to active missionary work. By 2002, Protestants as a combined group were estimated to account for approximately 15% of  the population, though some sources have placed this figure as high as 23% more recently.

subsections.title: Seventh -day Adventist Church
subsections.content:
- The Seventh -day Adventist Church operates one of only two private religious

schools in the country (alongside a Catholic school), with both schools open to members and non -members alike and subject to Ministry of Education curriculum oversight. Protestant l eaders, especially Seventh -day Adventist leaders, have demonstrated civic engagement —for example, participating in government COVID -19 awareness campaigns and broadcasting prevention messages. Freedom: São Tomé and Príncipe. https://www.state.gov/reports/2020 -report -on- international -religious -freedom/sao -tome -and-principe

subsections.title: Islam
subsections.content:
- The Muslim population of São Tomé and Príncipe is small but growing, estimated

at between 1% and 3% of the total population depending on the source and year. The U.S. State Department's World Religion Profile estimates 3% Muslim, while a 2012 CIA report rec ords approximately 3% as well. Most Muslims are migrants from Nigeria and Cameroon who have arrived over the last two decades. The proximity of the islands to the West African mainland has facilitated this immigration. https://www.thearda.com/world -religion/national -profiles?u=195c

subsections.title: Other Minor Faiths
subsections.content:
- Small communities of the Bahá'í Faith, Judaism (historically present since the 15th

century when thousands of Jewish children were forcibly deported to the island), Hinduism, and Buddhism also exist on the islands, comprising a combined share of approximate ly 0.1 –1% each. The Jewish community, though demographically negligible at 0.1% of the population according to the Pew Research Center, has left a lasting cultural imprint on Creole customs and traditions. Research Center data. from IndexMundi. https://www.indexmundi.com/sao_tome_and_principe/religions.html

subsections.title: Syncretic and Traditional African Beliefs
subsections.content:
- Despite over five centuries of Roman Catholic influence, traditional African beliefs

and practices remain widespread, often coexisting with nominal Christian affiliation. Black slaves brought to the islands from Benin, Gabon, the Republic of the Congo, and Angola introduced animism, totemism, and mortuary cults. Over centuries, these merged with Catholicism to produce syncretic expressions of faith. For instance, the notion of Sum d'Océ (meaning 'Lord of the Heavens') combines the Christian creator God with a controller of wealth drawn from African cosmology. Small plantation -era chapels combined Catholic crosses with African charms.  RELIGIOUS BREAKDOWN — SÃO TOMÉ AND PRÍNCIPE (2012 CIA EST.) Roman Catholic: 55.7% Seventh -day Adventist: 4.1% Assembly of God: 3.4% New Apostolic: 2.9% Mana Church: 2.3% Universal Kingdom of God: 2.0% Jehovah's Witnesses: 1.2% Other Christian: 6.2% No religion / Unaffiliated: 21.2% Unspecified: 1.0%

- A Melanesian belief system is also recorded, with followers constituting

approximately 2.9% of the total population. Reports also indicate that witchcraft - related persecution occurs on both islands —particularly targeting elderly women accused of 'fitxicêlu ' (witchcraft in the Forro language) —suggesting a persistent undercurrent of African spiritual worldview that orthodox Christian catechesis has historically not addressed adequately. International. https://fot.humanists.international/countries/africa -middle -africa/sao -tome -and- principe/ Encyclopedia.com. Op. cit.

sections.content:
- São Tomé and Príncipe is one of Africa's most thoroughly Christianized nations.

According to multiple authoritative sources, Christianity in one form or other accounts for approximately 97% of the total population's religious affiliation — making it an overwh elmingly Christian society with deep historical roots in Roman Catholicism inherited from five centuries of Portuguese colonial presence. Largest Religion. Retrieved March 2026.

subsections.title: Príncipe Island — Christian Population Estimate
subsections.content:
- Príncipe island has a much

smaller population —estimated at 9,830 by the Instituto Nacional de Estatística in 2024. The Autonomous Region of Príncipe shares the national religious profile, with Christianity (predominantly Catholic) as the faith of the vast majority. Applying the national religious proportions, the estimated Christian population on Príncipe is approximately 9,500 persons .

- While Príncipe's population is

small, it is geographically isolated and has historically received less attention from any denomination. The island has no airport with regular international connections and is accessible mainly via inter - island flights from São Tomé. A Coptic mission on Príncipe —even a periodic pastoral visit —would represent a unique and uncontested Christian witness. The isolation of Príncipe's community, its strong rural and close -knit identity, and the near -total absence of any non -Catholic Christian institution make it fertile ground for the Coptic Church's first outreach. Wikipedia. Op. cit.

subsections.title: The Unchurched and Syncretical Believing Population
subsections.content:
- Approximately 21.2% of the population identifies as having 'no religion', according

to the CIA's 2012 estimate. However, Encyclopedia  Britannica notes that 'about one-fifth of the population identifies as nonreligious' —these individuals, while not formally affiliated, often continue to participate in life -cycle rituals such as baptisms, funerals, and communal celebrations. This cohort r epresents a significant population open to re -evangelization.

- Additionally, those who practice syncretic blends of Catholicism and African

traditionalism represent a spiritually open demographic. The Coptic Orthodox Church's ancient African roots, its non -colonial identity, its rich patristic tradition, and its disti nctive liturgical practice could serve as powerful points of attraction for both the unchurched and the disillusioned within the existing Catholic community. https://www.britannica.com/place/Sao -Tome -and-Principe

subsections.title: Roman Catholic Church
subsections.content: The Roman Catholic Church remains the dominant and best -resourced religious organization in São Tomé and Príncipe. The country has a single diocese —the Diocese of São Tomé and Príncipe —headquartered in São Tomé city. The diocese was originally established i n 1534 as part of Portugal's Metropolitan Archdiocese of Funchal. The main Catholic church is the Cathedral of Our Lady of Grace in São Tomé, which bears the Cross of São Tomé as its ecclesiastical symbol. Since independence in 1975, the Church has been ru n primarily by expatriate priests. Catholic institutions include one private school (open to all). The Church exercises significant cultural influence through baptism, funerary rites, and patron saint festivals across all districts. https://www.worldatlas.com/articles/religion -in-sao-tome -and-principe.html

subsections.title: Protestant and Evangelical Organizations
subsections.content:
Protestant Christianity has grown markedly since independence. Key organizations currently operating in São Tomé and Príncipe include:

- Seventh -day Adventist Church (SDA): One of the two recognized private religious

schools; active in healthcare messaging and public awareness campaigns.

- Assembly of God: 3.4% of the national population; evangelical Pentecostal

background.

- New Apostolic Church: 2.9% of the population; increasingly active in urban areas.

- Universal Church of the Kingdom of God (UCKG): Has faced some incidents of

vandalism (2019); services resumed and facilities repaired by 2020.

- Jehovah's Witnesses: 1.2% of population; regular door -to-door outreach

activities.

- Thokoist  Church, Evangelical Assembly of Christ, Universal Church of Christ:

Smaller groups with a combined following of approximately 8,000 persons. Freedom: São Tomé and Príncipe. Op. cit.

subsections.title: Mana Church
subsections.content:
- The Mana Church, which originated in Lisbon, Portugal in 1984, has an established

presence in São Tomé and Príncipe representing approximately 2.3% of the population. The movement believes in supernatural forces and powers attributed to persons, spirits, an d natural objects, drawing on a syncretic blend of African traditionalism and Christian elements. It was brought to the islands by the Portuguese colonial network in a manner analogous to Catholicism. The Mana Church's appeal to supernatural and ancestral dimensions indicates that São Toméan Christians remain spiritually receptive to traditions that engage the

- mystical and transcendent —a dimension in which the Coptic Orthodox liturgical

and ascetic tradition is exceptionally strong.

subsections.title: Bahá'í Faith
subsections.content:
- The Bahá'í community in São Tomé and Príncipe has been growing steadily since

the late 20th century. Bahá'í missionaries have been active in the country, emphasizing education, social development, and interfaith dialogue. The Bahá'í community's model of com munity -building and its lack of formal clergy make its presence non -competitive with the Coptic Orthodox mission model.

subsections.title: Absence of Orthodox Christian Presence
subsections.content:
- Neither the Coptic Orthodox Church (Oriental Orthodox) nor the Greek Orthodox

Patriarchate of Alexandria and All Africa (Eastern Orthodox) have  any established presence in São Tomé and Príncipe. This is a remarkable gap, given that the Patriarchate of Alexandria has canonical jurisdiction over all African nations. The nearest Coptic Orthodox mission points are in Nigeria (Lagos and Calabar, estab lished 2005) and Cameroon (covered by the Metropolitan of Accra, who has jurisdiction over 22 West African countries). The Greek Orthodox Patriarchate of Alexandria has active missions in Ghana, Nigeria, and Cameroon but no presence recorded in São Tomé an d Príncipe. Orthodox Mission in Tropical Africa. Missions Institute of Orthodox Christianity. https://missions.hchc.edu/articles/articles/orthodox -mission -in-tropical -africa

sections.title: COPTIC ORTHODOX CHURCH — AFRICAN MISSION PRECEDENT

subsections.title: Historical Overview of Coptic Missions in Sub -Saharan Africa
subsections.content: The Coptic Orthodox Church of Alexandria holds canonical and historical primacy over all of Africa, having been founded by St. Mark the Evangelist in Alexandria in approximately AD 61. Since the demise of the Latin North African Archdiocese of Carthage in t he 8th century, Alexandria has been the sole Apostolic See with jurisdiction over the entire continent. The modern era of active Coptic mission in sub - Saharan Africa began in earnest in 1976 when His Grace Bishop Antonius Markos (Anthony Mark) was consecra ted by Pope Shenouda III as General Bishop for African Affairs and Patriarchal Exarch in West and South Africa. A second bishop, His Grace Bishop Paul (Boulos), was consecrated in the 1990s as General Bishop for Evangelism and Mission and Patriarchal Exarc h in East and Central Africa. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coptic_Orthodox_Church_in_Africa Coptic Mission. About Us. Op. cit.

subsections.title: Current Coptic Presence in West Africa — Closest Neighbors
subsections.content: The Coptic Church's closest established mission to São Tomé and Príncipe is in Nigeria, where the first Coptic Orthodox Church was established in Lagos in 2005. In 2006, four additional churches were established in Calabar, which has become the heart of the Nigerian Coptic community. The mission in Nigeria is served by rotating priests and deacons, with a dedicated Coptic Centre built in Calabar. Nigeria is geographically the closest jurisdiction to São Tomé and Príncipe (approximately 800 km), making it the most logical platform from which to support and sustain a new mission in São Tomé and Príncipe.

subsections.title: Parallels from Comparable Island Missions
subsections.content: The Coptic Church's successful establishment of missions in geographically isolated contexts offers instructive precedent for São Tomé and Príncipe. The mission in Madagascar —an island nation of comparable remoteness —was pioneered by Archimandrite Nectarios  Kellis in 1994, who began by personally visiting towns and villages to explain the Orthodox Christian faith. Within a short period, new congregations were established, liturgical services were translated into local languages, and a local priest was ordain ed. The Madagascar model —personal evangelism, liturgical inculturation, and rapid development of local clergy —is directly applicable to São Tomé and Príncipe. Orthodox Christianity. Op. cit.

subsections.title: The Organization of African Instituted Churches (OAIC) Connection
subsections.content:
- The Organization of African Instituted Churches (OAIC) was founded in 1978 at an

historic conference in Cairo convened by His Holiness Pope Shenouda III, upon the initiative of His Grace Bishop Markos. With chapters now operating in Kenya, Uganda, Tanzania,  Botswana, Zimbabwe, Western Cape, Eastern Cape, Ghana, Madagascar, Nigeria, and the Democratic Republic of Congo, the OAIC constitutes a pan -African ecumenical network through which the Coptic Church can make initial contact with local African Instituted Churches in São Tomé and Príncipe and use them as bridges for contextual outreach.
